case.case_title: Liverpool Navigation (Pvt) Limited v. Chandrananda De Silva, Secretary, Ministry of Defence and Others
case.source_citation: Sri Lanka Law Reports, 2000, 1 Sri LR, SC Application No 312/99 (FR), decided on 28 January 2000

clause.text: General restrictions may apply for national security, public order, health, morality, and welfare.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the refusal to grant security clearance for the petitioner's vessel to operate between Colombo and Jaffna, under Emergency Regulations, violated the petitioner's fundamental rights given the national security concerns under Article 15(7).
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner argued that the refusal to grant security clearance infringed its fundamental rights, particularly the right to equality under Article 12(1), as the vessel was prevented from operating and the petitioner was not given a lawful reason for the refusal.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the refusal was justified under the Emergency (Establishment of a Prohibited Zone) Regulations made under the Public Security Ordinance, which are valid laws restricting fundamental rights in the interest of national security as permitted by Article 15(7). They argued that the petitioner failed to disclose the true nature of the vessel charter and that there were serious security concerns, including investigations into the chairman's alleged involvement in illegal activities potentially linked to the LTTE.
key_facts: Certain areas in the North and East were declared Prohibited Zones under Emergency Regulations.
Security clearance was required to enter these zones and was refused for the petitioner's vessel.
The petitioner failed to disclose the true nature of the charter party, which was found to be a sham.
The chairman of the petitioner company was under CID investigation for alleged illegal foreign currency transfers possibly funding LTTE arms.
The petitioner made multiple changes to its board of directors, which the respondents viewed as suspicious.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court held that Article 15(7) permits restrictions on fundamental rights by law in the interests of national security, including regulations made under the Public Security Ordinance. The Court recognized the grave security situation in the North and East and accepted that national security is a predominant factor in decisions regarding security clearance.
reasoning.application_to_facts: Given the ongoing investigations and the petitioner's failure to disclose material facts, the Court found no arbitrary or mala fide conduct by the respondents. The refusal to grant security clearance was a lawful restriction under Article 15(7) and the Emergency Regulations, justified by national security concerns.
principles_established: Restrictions on fundamental rights under Article 15(7) are valid if prescribed by law in the interests of national security.
The executive's concerns regarding national security must be given due consideration by the courts.
The Court will not interfere with executive discretion on national security unless it is shown to be unreasonable or mala fide.
The Emergency Regulations are valid laws under Article 15(7) permitting restrictions in Prohibited Zones.
precedents_cited: Tennakoon v. T.P.F. de Silva and Others (1997) 3 Sri LR 16
Premachandra v. Jayawickrama and Another (1994) 2 Sri LR 90
Council of Civil Service Unions and Others v. Minister for the Civil Service (1984) 3 ALL ER. 935

outcome.holding: The Court dismissed the petitioner's fundamental rights application, holding that the refusal to grant security clearance was a lawful restriction under Article 15(7) justified by national security concerns.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 15(7) was central to the Court's reasoning as it authorizes lawful restrictions on fundamental rights in the interests of national security, which justified the Emergency Regulations and the refusal of security clearance.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The Court noted that Article 15(7) permits restrictions prescribed by law in the interests of national security, including regulations under the Public Security Ordinance, and that the Emergency Regulations were made in the interests of national security. The petitioner failed to disclose the true nature of the vessel charter and the chairman was under investigation for activities potentially threatening national security.
